brief.title: Find 13 without checking every number
brief.learner: Can compare whole numbers; has not studied search algorithms.
brief.goal: Explain why sorted order allows a comparison to rule out half of the remaining candidates.

instruction: Apply library principles before choosing cards. Carry relevant prior knowledge forward, author one causal story, and choose an intuition boundary with article reading destinations. Introduce prerequisites before using them. Specify visual capabilities, never renderer names. Establish a whole-lesson visual vocabulary before implementing motion; capability matching alone is insufficient.

principles.status: User-approved design direction; not a measured claim of learning effectiveness.
principles.precedence: Apply these principles before individual cards. Cards are optional techniques within one connected lesson, not a requirement to animate every topic.

teaching.title: Carry learning forward
teaching.rule: Identify what the learner knows from earlier parts. Briefly recall the relevant model and explicitly connect each new idea to it. Not having read this article does not mean knowing nothing.
teaching.check: Can the learner say what stayed the same and what this part adds?

teaching.title: Teach one connected problem
teaching.rule: Organize the lesson as a causal chain: familiar system, limitation, change, consequences, resolution. Explain why later sections follow from earlier ones.
teaching.check: Can the learner explain why this section is needed in the same story?

teaching.title: Intuition before completeness
teaching.rule: Choose the few relationships needed to understand the article. Leave exact code, exhaustive cases, derivations, and mechanics to clearly identified reading destinations. Do not animate every paragraph.
teaching.check: Can the learner state the big idea, then locate its details in the source?

teaching.title: Earn new terms and representations
teaching.rule: Show the concrete meaning before relying on its name or symbol. Explain changes of abstraction, simplifications, and departures from previous parts when they occur.
teaching.check: Can the learner connect the new term or picture to something already understood?

teaching.title: Overview, then guided attention
teaching.rule: For a multi-step process, establish its high-level purpose first. Keep a compact progress map beside the sequence. Wink points out the current causal change; additional prose lives behind its explanation.
teaching.check: Does the reader know both where to look and how that moment fits the whole?

teaching.title: Check understanding selectively
teaching.rule: Use a prediction or explanation only when it tests the central relationship using established knowledge. Offer a reveal; avoid compulsory quizzes on every detail.
teaching.check: Does the answer require reasoning about the model rather than recalling a label?

animation.title: One visual vocabulary for the whole lesson
animation.rule: Define each concept’s shape, label, color role, and identity before selecting motion techniques. Reuse that meaning across sections. Distinct concepts need distinguishable representations, not the same generic circle.
animation.check: Can the reader recognize the concept without relearning the legend?

animation.title: Use shape and labels as well as color
animation.rule: Color reinforces identity; it is not the only distinction. Keep identity colors separate from transient emphasis or state. Related instances can share a shape with different labels.
animation.check: Are process, socket, handle, record, and notification still distinguishable without color?

animation.title: Preserve the same system through change
animation.rule: Keep object identities and spatial anchors when useful. Show what changes and what remains. Explain any remapping; replay or zoom-out must be announced.
animation.check: Can the reader follow the same object before and after the change?

animation.title: Motion must explain the relationship
animation.rule: Aim for the main idea to be graspable in roughly ten seconds of viewing. Use transfer, separation, overlap, release, or collection to show causality. Text adds detail; prose appearing in boxes is not the main demonstration.
animation.check: After a short viewing, can the reader describe what happened without reading a paragraph?

animation.title: Reveal only what this moment needs
animation.rule: Do not visualize every detail or keep a growing text history on screen. Preserve essential context in the diagram and compact map; disclose secondary details on demand.
animation.check: Does every visible element help identify the current change or its context?

animation.title: Wink guides the actual focus
animation.rule: Place Wink beside the object being discussed. Keep mascot and speech clear of objects, labels, and paths. On narrow screens speech may dock below while Wink stays with the target.
animation.check: Can the learner immediately locate the important element without it being obscured?

animation.title: Pace for observation and control
animation.rule: Use six-second guided stops as the current prototype default, with manual stepping, replay, pause, and reduced-motion support. Preserve causal order; do not imply a total ordering of concurrent events.
animation.check: Can the learner pause and revisit the change without losing the story?

principles.scope_note: These are our design rules informed by the user’s feedback and the 16-chapter text-and-figure review. They are not a universal color system attributed to 3Blue1Brown.

teaching_examples.title: Expose the limit of the first approach
teaching_examples.before: The learner understands a simple way to do the task.
teaching_examples.after: They can explain why a change is needed.
sequence: Try the simple approach on one concrete case.
Show where it stops meeting the goal.
Change the part responsible for that limitation.
Carry the changed system forward: explain the new responsibilities or consequences it creates.

source.title: The paradox of the derivative
source.locator: Position and Velocity → Rates of Change

teaching_examples.observation: The lesson contrasts speed at an instant with measurements across two times, then examines shorter intervals.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A limitation gives the next idea a reason to exist; that structure can transfer beyond calculus.
teaching_examples.example: A single car snapshot cannot reveal its speed. Comparing two times provides the missing information.
avoid: Changing the task while comparing solutions.
Restarting with an unrelated model to explain the consequences of the change.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner identify which part of the first approach causes the limitation?

teaching_examples.title: Ask for a prediction, then explain the outcome
teaching_examples.before: The learner has seen a relationship in one case.
teaching_examples.after: They can use that relationship in a changed case.
sequence: Ask one answerable prediction.
Let the learner commit or choose to reveal.
Explain why the result follows, including incorrect answers.

source.title: The paradox of the derivative
source.locator: Position and Velocity → Rates of Change

teaching_examples.observation: The page asks readers to infer motion from a graph and includes a question about a negative tangent slope.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A prediction makes an otherwise invisible misunderstanding observable.
teaching_examples.example: A learner predicts which part of a journey has the greatest speed before seeing the corresponding velocity.
avoid: Testing a fact that has not been introduced.
Treating a correct guess as proof of understanding.
Adding compulsory predictions for every implementation detail.
teaching_examples.check: Ask for a reason or a new case, not only the answer.

teaching_examples.title: Start with something the learner can already judge
teaching_examples.before: The learner has relevant knowledge from earlier lessons or everyday experience; establish which applies.
teaching_examples.after: They can state the question in their own words.
sequence: Recall the relevant model from previous parts; offer a short refresher if needed.
Introduce one specific question that this known model does not yet answer.
State what carries forward and what new relationship this section will add.

source.title: Grant Sanderson — advice for making explanations
source.locator: FAQ: advice for making math videos

teaching_examples.observation: Sanderson recommends examples before general frameworks and putting the key exercise near the opening.
teaching_examples.interpretation: Begin with a judgment the learner can make before asking them to adopt new terminology.
teaching_examples.example: Recall browser → server → WSGI application before asking how several visitors can be served.
avoid: Assuming everyday experience supplies technical understanding.
Using a story that adds more unfamiliar things than it explains.
Resetting the learner to zero at each chapter.
Treating no prior article reading as no prior knowledge.
teaching_examples.check: Can a beginner describe the problem without using the new term?

teaching_examples.title: Give the idea a name after the learner has met it
teaching_examples.before: The learner has seen a concrete relationship.
teaching_examples.after: A new term names something recognizable.
sequence: Recall the concrete example.
Identify the shared relationship.
Introduce the conventional name with its scope.
If the representation changes, map the new picture back to the old one explicitly.

source.title: Grant Sanderson — advice for making explanations
source.locator: FAQ: advice for making math videos

teaching_examples.observation: Sanderson warns that pedagogical ordering can differ from the order in which definitions are normally presented.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A name should compress an idea the learner has already encountered.
teaching_examples.example: After seeing work overlap, introduce concurrency as the name for that overlap.
avoid: Replacing a missing explanation with a glossary.
Introducing several dependent terms at once.
Changing a symbol’s meaning silently between chapters.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner point to an instance of the named idea?

teaching_examples.title: Build the next idea from the same model
teaching_examples.before: The learner recognizes the system and its earlier behavior.
teaching_examples.after: They can explain why the next topic follows from the previous one.
sequence: Recall the relevant earlier relationship.
Introduce the smallest change that answers the current question.
Follow its consequences in the same story.
teaching_examples.observation: The opening explicitly recalls transformations, determinants, linear systems, and change of basis.
teaching_examples.interpretation: Treat prerequisites as reusable mental models; explicitly connect later difficulties to earlier changes.
teaching_examples.example: Adding a worker leads to two follow-up questions: who still has socket access, and what remains after the worker exits?
avoid: An isolated demonstration for every concept.
Leaving the connection to previous parts until the final exercise.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner explain why this chapter comes next?

review.interpretation: user-approved design direction; application needs learner review

teaching_examples.title: Set the boundary at useful intuition
teaching_examples.before: The source contains more detail than the reader needs for a first mental picture.
teaching_examples.after: They understand the main relationship and know what to read next.
sequence: Choose one high-level takeaway.
Show the smallest example that explains it.
Point to the source for mechanics, exact cases, and deeper study.

source.title: Inverse matrices, column space, and null space

teaching_examples.observation: The lesson explicitly prioritizes intuition and leaves computational methods to other resources.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A guide can make later reading easier without reproducing a complete technical course.
teaching_examples.example: Show why exit records need collecting; leave the exact waitpid return cases to the article.
avoid: Treating article coverage as a checklist of required animations.
Omitting a fact that would make the high-level picture misleading.
teaching_examples.check: Can the reader state the main idea and identify where to deepen it?

review.interpretation: user-approved design direction; application needs learner review

teaching_examples.title: Keep the current step connected to the whole
teaching_examples.before: The reader knows the goal but can lose their place in a sequence.
teaching_examples.after: They know the role of the current change in the whole process.
sequence: Introduce a small overview using familiar roles.
Keep a compact progress map while revealing one change.
Use Wink to direct attention; disclose extra explanation on demand.

source.title: Linear combinations, span, and basis vectors

teaching_examples.observation: The lesson explains the mapping from individual arrows to points and collections before using that shorthand.
teaching_examples.interpretation: Our overview-and-Wink adaptation keeps a sequence legible while making changes of representation explicit.
teaching_examples.example: Keep the request lifecycle visible while Wink points to the handle currently being released.
avoid: An overview crowded with unexplained technical terms.
Leaving the learner to infer the story from motion alone.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner say where they are and why this change matters?

review.interpretation: user-approved design direction; application needs learner review
